#4644. "What Does This Mean For Me?" When Life Is All About Ourself

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

This is part 2 in a series. You can read part 1 here.

We don't interact with our life directly; we interact with what life means about us. What if the problem isn't that life isn't meeting our needs? What if the problem is that getting our personal needs met has become the single focus of our life?

In part 1 of this series, I discussed the many ways we’re conditioned and wired to be self-focused in today’s world, to constantly monitor and manage our own okay-ness and whether our needs are being met. And furthermore, how each moment is experienced as what we've decided it says about us. Does this situation, conversation, decision, opinion make me feel less than or better than? Does it make me feel valued, comfortable, seen? Does it validate my story of “who I am”? I posited the idea that viewing our lives through the lens of “does this serve me?” is, at its root, an attempt to be happy, shore ourselves up, and ultimately, survive. While, in fact, we’ve got it wrong: putting “me” at the center of the universe and the reason everything happens ends up making us suffer.

So what exactly is the suffering that comes with our relentless self-focus—what’s wrong with seeing everything through the lens of how it affects “me”?

When we experience every situation and everyone else's choices through the lens of “self,” as fundamentally a commentary on how we're doing and a referendum on our worth, then every moment carries the potential to wound, undermine, humiliate, and destroy us. Every interaction can threaten who we think we are. We have to remain hyper-vigilant, therefore, on high alert for whether we’re okay or not okay, and any experience that feels like it doesn’t support our story of ourselves, which can also include a simple difference of opinion.

We live in a constant state of “not-enoughness.” We can never get enough approval, recognition, validation, reassurance, success, or reflection. The self that needs to be continually affirmed is never permanently satisfied; whatever we “get” only lasts as long as this particular experience. We imagine that if we win this argument or get this situation to “go our way,” and be “good for us,” we’ll finally get enough affirmation, enough validation to trust our worth and put down our “me” sword. But it never happens; there is no “enough” point, and so we live in a constant state of lack, always trying to get what we need from the outside so we can be okay on the inside.

Our life becomes an endless project dedicated to self-management.

We feel like we have to be constantly improving the project of "me"—making sure we're doing enough and getting enough. Our life becomes a full-time job of managing the person we're trying to be and be seen as. The result is utter exhaustion and burnout.

Because we experience other people as threats to our self-story, and see others through the lens of whether their behavior serves or doesn’t serve us, we can’t meet people for real, as they are. We’ve got too much skin in the game. Who they are becomes about who they make us feel we are. And so, we can’t really relax fully and get to know others and give them the space to be who they are as whole beings, independent from us, with their own motivations, desires, wants, and needs that are not about us. All roads lead back to us in some way, which clouds our view of the other. We can’t really listen because we have to constantly monitor and scan for potential threats to who we are. We can’t allow others to have a different opinion or experience from us because it “means” our opinion is wrong and consequently, there’s something wrong with us. Our “me” agenda requires everyone else’s thoughts, opinions, and truth to confirm and align with our “me” project, which is a lot of work since that’s never the case. That said, only some parts of other people are allowed into our relationships, the parts that work for us and give us what we need. But we’re not available to meet or know the whole of them.

Our relationships are, therefore, built on filling our own holes and reassuring our own insecurities—getting what we need to feel good or at least okay. We end up using other people to satisfy and validate ourselves. We give in order to feel appreciated and be valued as helpful. We listen to others in order to be perceived as a good listener and so that we can be listened to. How we relate is driven by how it relates to and reflects on us. Our relationships, therefore, can’t be truly open, honest, and emotionally intimate; we can’t be vulnerable and undefended, and can’t really know others as people in their own right, who they really are separate from us. We remain disconnected, relating to others as merely supporting characters in our personal movie—the movie playing in our me-focused mind.

Because we’re always telling ourselves a story about our life, what it means for us, whether we’re getting what we need, and whether our life is serving the project of “me,” we’re not available to life as it’s actually happening. We’re not in the present moment; we're trapped inside a story we’ve told ourselves about our life and how our “me” is faring in it. At the same time, we’re not truly connected to other people. Other people are characters in our personal movie, and are experienced through the lens of whether they’re filling our needs and making us feel good about ourselves. Other people are not subjects in their own right, but objects who can help support who we think we are.

Our self-focused approach to life is an attempt to keep us happy and secure, but it ends up backfiring, leaving us feeling disconnected from life and other people, enslaved to how we're being perceived. It leaves us defensive and emotionally fragile, vulnerable to other people’s different opinions and experiences, and having to constantly manage the project of “me” and make sure we’re enough.

In part 3, I’ll dive into the profound benefits of dropping “me” from the center of our universe, and the relief that comes when we learn to show up for life without our “me” in the way, and when we can see life as something happening, but without turning it into something happening to, for, and because of us. What if it’s not about us?

#4643. Why Living with Endometriosis May Double Your Odds of Migraine

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

In a new analysis, researchers found females with endometriosis were 2.3 times more likely to also have migraine, and they said the two conditions may share a pain pathway involving nerves and inflammation.Recognizing that connection earlier could lead to coordinated care for both conditions, the researchers said.The analysis, presented at the American Neurological Association (ANA) Annual Meeting in San Diego on October 20, included more than 13 million females. The research hasn’t yet been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

Endometriosis occurs when tissue similar to what lines the uterus grows outside the uterus, Mallory Stuparich, MD, a gynecologic surgeon at MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, California, told Healthline. Stuparich was not involved in the study.Yohannes Woubishet Woldeamanuel, MD, lead author of the study and assistant professor of neurology at Mayo Clinic Arizona, told Healthline that migraine also involves more than one part of the body.“Migraine is more than a headache,” he said.Headache is one symptom, Woldeamanuel said, but migraine can also cause sensory, motor, and balance symptoms.“Migraine is a little complex. It’s a multiple-nervous system involving a condition,” he said.

Stuparich said endometriosis pain typically develops in 2 ways. The first starts in the lesions themselves.“There are inflammatory markers that are created by the endometriosis lesions themselves, and those inflammatory markers can irritate the nerves that live close by the lesions,” she said.The second involves the nervous system, Stuparich said. Scar tissue can grow its own nerve supply, and years of chronic pain can change how the nervous system responds. That adaptation can “perpetuate pain or make people feel sensations that normally wouldn’t be painful,” she said.Stuparich said the inflammatory and immune processes involved in endometriosis have “pretty significant overlap in the setting of migraines.”

One possible link between the two conditions is calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), a chemical messenger that helps transmit pain signals, the researchers said.CGRP plays a key role in migraine attacks, Woldeamanuel said, and blocking it reduces those attacks. CGRP medications work by blocking the sites where CGRP attaches or by binding to CGRP itself.Researchers have also found CGRP in endometriosis tissue.

A 2024 study published in Science Translational Medicine found CGRP in endometriosis lesions from both people and mice. In mice, blocking CGRP signaling reduced pain and reduced lesion size.

Other studies point to shared biology between the two conditions:

Stuparich said she was “not surprised at all” by the finding because it matches what she sees in her own patients.“We see this overlap of patients who have endometriosis also having migraines,” she said.Stuparich said the science still has gaps. She noted that nothing has been proven conclusively in peer-reviewed research yet, but the way both diseases behave supports a connection.“It makes sense that there would be overlap,” she said.

Endometriosis and migraine are treated by different specialists, so the overlap is easy to miss, Woldeamanuel said.For the analysis, researchers at Mayo Clinic Arizona reviewed 35 studies published over 50 years, comparing migraine rates among 207,675 females with endometriosis and 12,963,120 females without the condition.Short-term health records miss up to 90% of that overlap, according to the analysis. Migraine rates in females with endometriosis changed depending on how each study identified migraine.“This data is hiding,” Woldeamanuel said.

“These two clinics are siloed. One clinic doesn’t ask about the other condition. They just focus on their own specialty,” Woldeamanuel said.The findings of the analysis have not been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

Some treatments already overlap, Stuparich said. Hormonal birth control “can sometimes be used to treat menstrually associated migraines,” she said.Stuparich said she has heard anecdotally of patients whose endometriosis symptoms improved after they started CGRP medications for migraine, though long-term data are still lacking.The researchers said the findings support studying whether existing CGRP-blocking migraine medications could also relieve endometriosis pain, potentially offering one treatment for both conditions.Woldeamanuel leads a planned Mayo Clinic trial testing one of those medications, rimegepant (Nurtec ODT), for endometriosis pain. The trial will also track migraine days in participants who have both conditions. It’s expected to finish in 2031, according to ClinicalTrials.gov.

People who suspect they have both conditions can take steps now to get them treated together, Stuparich said.Patients can raise the connection themselves, Stuparich said. She suggested a starting point for each appointment:

Patients can also ask for an early referral to the other specialist so both conditions get coordinated care, Woldeamanuel said. “The earlier it’s diagnosed, the better it’s managed,” he said.Stuparich said doctors are moving away from viewing endometriosis as only a gynecologic disorder because it can affect the whole body.“It is a whole body systemic neuroinflammatory neuroimmune disorder,” she said.

#4642. Tesla Model X on Autopilot/FSD hit a pole and flipped, killing passenger

A Tesla Model X veered off Golden Gate Parkway in Naples, Florida, hit a traffic signal pole and overturned in September, killing a 50-year-old woman riding as a passenger. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged.

Tesla flagged this crash itself, through its telematics, and says it has the car’s event data recorder and video. The public was told a car “veered off the road.” It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

At 11:43 p.m. on Wednesday, September 30, 2026, a 2025 Tesla Model X was heading east on Golden Gate Parkway in Collier County, approaching the Estuary Boulevard intersection, according to a Florida Highway Patrol press release.

The SUV left the road, hit a traffic signal pole on the corner of the intersection, and rolled over. Its passenger, a 50-year-old woman from Fort Myers, was pronounced dead at the scene. The 48-year-old driver, also from Fort Myers, went to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

FHP said the crash remains under investigation. It hasn’t released the woman’s name, a cause, or anything about speed or impairment. And nothing about a driver-assist system.

Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

It identifies a 2025 Model X and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged,” meaning Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 39 mph, a collision with a pole or tree, airbag deployment, and damage to the front and the top of the car, which fits FHP’s account of the rollover.

This record is unusually complete on what Tesla has. It checks the event data recorder, telematics, video, and “other.” And it says Tesla learned of the crash through its own telematics, not just from the media.

Then it redacts the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 03:41 UTC on October 1, which is 11:41 p.m. in Florida on September 30, two minutes off FHP’s 11:43 p.m. The city, the 2025 Model X, the pole, and the fatal outcome all line up. Because the UTC timestamp crosses midnight, Tesla’s record lists the crash in October, so anyone checking Tesla’s data against September crashes would miss it. It’s the same crash.

Most of the crashes we’ve matched leave real gaps in what Tesla holds. Not this one. Tesla has the video, the EDR, and the telematics, and it knew about the crash on its own.

So Tesla can see what the car did on the approach to that intersection. It knows whether the system steered the SUV off the road or the driver did, whether the car warned him, and how fast it was going when it hit the pole. It filed all of that under a redaction.

Autopilot/FSD might not have caused the crash, but it was active within 30 seconds of the crash, so it’s important to understand what happened. Was the driver distracted? Did Autopilot/FSD make a run move?

There’s also a living witness here. The driver survived with non-life-threatening injuries, which means FHP can ask him whether he had Autopilot or FSD on and what the car was doing. We don’t know if anyone has. Troopers may not even know Tesla verified the system was engaged.

This is the second fatal Tesla driver-assist crash in Naples in this NHTSA release. In May, a Model 3 with the system engaged at 71 mph hit an overturned box truck on I-75 at Pine Ridge Road, killing three people. FHP investigated both, and neither crash was ever publicly tied to Autopilot or FSD.

The same release set a new record: 264 Tesla driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236.

This is the cleanest example yet of how much Tesla knows and how little it shares. It detected the crash on its own. It has the video. It has the EDR. A woman riding as a passenger died in a Model X that, according to Tesla, had its driver-assist engaged. And the public account is one sentence: the car veered off the road.

Tesla certainly benefits by keeping the information hidden. Most are willing to look past these things and not be suspicious, but ultimately the question is why hide. something if you dont have something to hide.

We’re not saying the system caused this crash. We don’t know, and that’s the point. Tesla does know, and it decided the account of what its car did in a fatal crash is a trade secret.

If FSD or Autopilot did nothing wrong here, Tesla has the footage to prove it. It was happy to share data in the Katy crash when it helped its case. When Tesla keeps the video sealed, people are going to assume the worst, and Tesla only has itself to blame.

We’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol whether its investigators knew the system was engaged and whether they got Tesla’s video and raw data, or only Tesla’s interpretation of them. Same questions we asked about Vineland. How many more fatal crashes will troopers close without knowing what Tesla knows?

#4641. ADHD Medications May Help Ease Menopausal Brain Fog

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Medications commonly used to treat attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may help reduce certain symptoms of menopausal brain fog, according to a review presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The research suggests that both lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) and atomoxetine (Strattera) may improve self-reported executive function in perimenopausal and postmenopausal people. However, they showed little to no effect on objective cognitive tests.

While this scoping review showed promising results, experts caution that it may be too early to begin recommending these medications to females experiencing menopause.

Sara Vaughn, MD, Chief Medical Officer at Clair Health, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are interesting and hypothesis-generating, but they do not yet establish ADHD medications as a treatment for menopausal brain fog.

Many middle-aged females report experiencing forgetfulness, slow thinking, reduced concentration, and difficulty finding words. This is often referred to as “brain fog,” and is a common occurrence during various stages of menopause.

These symptoms of brain fog also mirror the symptoms of ADHD.

Brain fog may be due to declining or fluctuating levels of estrogen during perimenopause, which affects dopamine and norepinephrine signaling in the prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus. This can impact memory, focus, and executive functioning.

Despite how disruptive these symptoms can be to quality of life, there is currently no medication approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to manage them. This often leaves clinicians in a position of trying to differentiate between brain fog from menopause and undiagnosed ADHD.

The review analyzed five studies involving females ages 45–60 with their last menstrual period within the past 10 years. The studies all focused on how ADHD medications affect outcome measures of cognition and ADHD severity.

The researchers found that with lisdexamfetamine, scores on the Brown Attention Deficit Disorder Scale (BADDS), a self-report rating scale that measures ADHD symptoms, dropped from 35.7 to 21.2, compared with 29.8 with a placebo. With atomoxetine, BADDS scores decreased from 38.6 to 25.5, compared with 30.1 with a placebo.

There was no significant benefit observed on objective cognitive tests (ex., memory and processing speed).

These findings suggest that certain ADHD medications may improve perceived cognitive symptoms during menopause, although benefits were not demonstrated on objective cognitive tests.

Jennifer Tat, a medical student at the University of Tennessee Health Sciences Center and lead author of the study, noted, “In the population data, symptom severity, not a formal ADHD diagnosis, predicted menopausal burden. Many women were never diagnosed, so relying on a chart diagnosis misses the women most at risk.”

“We have evidence that the menopause transition is associated with measurable brain changes,” said Vaughn. “But no specific brain signature of menopausal brain fog has been established. To study it rigorously, we first need to define what the term means and measure it consistently.”

Limitations of this review include the small number of studies and the small sample sizes. Most of the measures were also self-reported, which leaves room for error.

Also, the FDA has not approved these types of medications for menopausal brain fog, meaning using them for these purposes would be off-label.

“ADHD medications are not without risks, and I think it is too early to use them routinely for menopausal ‘brain fog,’” said Vaughn.

ADHD medications can carry risks, including cardiovascular side effects. Stimulants such as lisdexamfetamine also have the potential for misuse and dependence. These medications should only be used with medical supervision.

“I am a strong proponent of treating the underlying disorder rather than treating isolated symptoms. ADHD and menopausal cognitive symptoms may look alike, but that does not mean they share the same underlying mechanism—or require the same treatment,” noted Vaughn.

Further research, including additional long-term prospective studies, is needed before clinical guidance can be changed

“We hope this opens up the conversations with patients and providers. We recommend clinicians to screen patients for ADHD and, for those who screen positive, refer them to our psychiatric colleagues who have the knowledge and resources to perform a diagnostic test so that those women who have gone undiagnosed with ADHD can get the treatment they need and deserve,” said Tat.

According to the National Council on Aging (NCOA), your brain requires exercise to function optimally, just like your muscles do.

Ways to help keep your brain sharp and manage menopausal brain fog include:

The NCOA also suggests keeping your brain well-exercised by:

You can also speak with your healthcare professional about how menopause, estrogen levels, hormone therapy, and modifiable risk factors like a sedentary lifestyle or high blood pressure can affect cognitive health.

“I want clinicians to know that they must take brain fog seriously. Ask whether the symptoms are new or a lifelong pattern that menopause has worsened. ADHD in women often goes unrecognized for decades,” said Tat.

#4639. The Boon of Being Highly Sensitive

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

Are you more easily overstimulated than others by what’s going on around you? Maybe you’re easily distracted or stressed by loud noises (it’s the kitchen exhaust fan for me), bright artificial lighting, uncomfortable clothing, or other people’s moods. If so, you may be among the 30% of people who are highly sensitive to sensory input from the environment.

We all navigate the world using our senses. It’s just that some of us seem to take in more and be more impacted by what we take in. Scientists are still making discoveries about sensory processing in different situations and for different people.

Here’s a fascinating example — did you know that human hands can sense the presence of something without touching it? Last year, a group of researchers published the first study demonstrating remote sensing in humans (Chen, Crucianelli, Versace, & Jamone, 2025). Participants in their study were able to detect that an object was buried in sand when their fingers were still 6.9 cm away from the object. How? Humans can perceive subtle changes in the sand caused by the object. What’s even more incredible is that humans were 30% more accurate than robotic sensors. Specifically, the robotic sensors had more false positives (“sensing” an object when there was not one). The researchers suspect humans are better able to interpret touch sensations because our nervous systems are designed to filter noise, weigh uncertainty, and make decisions about ambiguous situations.

Clearly, there's still a lot to learn about sensory processing in humans. These days, it’s widely accepted that some of us are more sensitive to the environment than others. As we understand more about sensory sensitivity, more research is focusing on an idea intuitive to many of us: sensory processing sensitivity comes with great benefits.

Dr. Elaine Aron began researching sensory processing sensitivity (SPS; also called high sensitivity) in 1991. SPS is well summarized as “lower sensory thresholds, susceptibility to overstimulation, deeper processing of environmental information, heightened emotional and physiological reactivity, and increased awareness of subtle stimuli” (Weyn, Greven, Schmidt, Gillebert, 2025).

SPS isn't a diagnosis. It's a normally distributed personality trait or aspect of temperament. This means we all fall somewhere on the sensitivity continuum. While 20-30% of us are highly sensitive, 40-50% of us are moderately sensitive, and 20-30% of us have low sensitivity (Lionetti et al. 2018). Evolutionary theories suggest there is an advantage for humans if some of us (not too many) are highly sensitive (Greven et al. 2019).

Sensory sensitivity is heritable. Studies have found that 47% of the variability in sensory sensitivity is explained by genetics (Assary, 2020). It’s also biologically based. Neuroimaging studies have found that folks with SPS have greater activation in brain areas involved in sensory processing (e.g., awareness, integration, empathy, preparation for action, higher-order visual processing).

Sensory processing sensitivity is typically measured using the Highly Sensitive Person Scale, which was revised earlier this year (Pluess et al. 2026). It's an 18-item questionnaire that captures six domains of sensitivity: 1. sensitivity to details 2. depth of processing 3. social sensitivity 4. sensitivity to positive experiences 5. emotional reactivity and 6. overstimulation.

If you (or someone you’re close to) has high sensory sensitivity, you don’t need me to tell you about its challenges, which can include overstimulation, exhaustion, and stress. What might not be top of mind are the benefits that can come along with high SPS. You may be surprised to learn that folks who have high SPS may actually be better positioned to thrive in supportive, positive environments (Damatac et al. 2025).

If you’re someone who is more easily overstimulated by unpleasant sensory input like the kitchen fan, you’re likely also more easily positively influenced by positive input such as a view of the gorgeous fall leaves. And the positive benefit is likely to be longer-lasting. This makes logical sense. It’s also been supported by the research. In one example, Lionette et al. (2018) found that folks who had high SPS had a more positive response to happy video clips as compared with people who had lower sensory sensitivity. Research has also found that folks with high SPS can actually experience more benefit from psychological interventions and social support as compared with people with lower SPS (Damatac, et al. 2025; Nocentini, Menesini, & Pluess 2018).

This sensitivity to positive experiences overlaps with another dimension of SPS — aesthetic sensitivity. Aesthetic sensitivity describes the deep emotional and physiological response to beauty, art, and nature often experienced by folks who are highly sensitive.

Chacón et al. (2024) found aesthetic sensitivity among folks with high SPS strongly correlated with the personality traits openness and agreeableness (a replication of previous findings), as well as adaptive coping strategies including emotional expression and regulation. They found that folks with high SPS and high aesthetic sensitivity more effectively navigated emotionally dysregulating challenges in daily living, such as problematic situations at work.

Another recent study found that folks with sensory sensitivity demonstrated higher cognitive flexibility, which is associated with adaptive coping and problem-solving (Shippers, Hoogman & Greven, 2025). The study also found that folks with high SPS who were more sensitive to aesthetic beauty scored higher on measures of curiosity and humor.

If you’re highly sensitive, you're likely more inclined toward creativity and empathy. Laros-van Gorkom et al. (2025) found that folks with high sensory sensitivity are more likely to be more empathic and more likely to have creative ideas. In their study, folks with high aesthetic sensitivity were more likely to engage in creative activities.

Those of us who have high sensory sensitivity experience awe more frequently. For example, Dunne et al (2024) found that folks with high SPS were more likely to experience a profound emotional and physiological response to the beauty of nature. This experience of awe directs attention away from ourselves and toward our natural surroundings, which deepens our connection to the natural world. The experience of awe is widely known to enhance well-being.

This rally around the advantages of SPS is extremely encouraging. It confirms that sensory sensitivity can be a strength promoting well-being. In positive environments, folks with SPS are actually uniquely positioned to flourish.

Assary, E., Zavos, H.M.S., Krapohl, E. et al. (2021). Genetic architecture of Environmental Sensitivity reflects multiple heritable components: a twin study with adolescents. Mol Psychiatry 26, 4896–4904.

Chacón, A., Borda-Mas, M., Rivera, F., Pérez-Chacón, M., and Avargues-Navarro, M.L. (2024) Aesthetic sensitivity: relationship with openness to experience and agreeableness, health-related quality of life and adaptive coping strategies in people with high sensory processing sensitivity. Front. Psychol., 14.

Chen, Z., Crucianelli, L., Versace E., and Jamone, L. (2025) Exploring Tactile Perception for Object Localization in Granular Media: A Human and Robotic Study, 2025 IEEE International Conference on Development and Learning (ICDL), Prague, Czech Republic.

Damatac, C., ter Avest, M., Wilderjans, T., De Gucht, V., Woestenburg, D., Landeweerd, L., Galesloot, T., Geerligs, L., Homberg, J., Greven, C. (2025). Exploring sensory processing sensitivity: Relationships with mental and somatic health, interactions with positive and negative environments, and evidence for differential susceptibility, Current Research in Behavioral Sciences, 8.

Dunne, H. Lionetti, F., Pluess, M., Setti, A. (2024). Individual traits are associated with pro-environmental behaviour: Environmental sensitivity, nature connectedness and consideration for future consequences. People and Nature, 6, 586-597.

Greven, C., Lionetti, F., Booth, C., Aron, E.N., Fox, E., Schendan, H.E., Pluess, M., Bruining, H., Acevedo, B., Bijttebier, P., Homberg, J. (2019). Sensory Processing Sensitivity in the context of Environmental Sensitivity: A critical review and development of research agenda,Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews, 98, 287-305,

Laros-van Gorkom, B.A.P., Damatac, C.G., Stevelmans, I., and Greven, C.U. (2025) Relationships of sensory processing sensitivity with creativity and empathy in an adult sample. Front. Psychol., 15.

Lionetti, F., Aron, A., Aron, E.N., Burns, G.L., Jagiellowicz, J., Pluess, M. (2018) Dandelions, tulips and orchids: evidence for the existence of low-sensitive, medium-sensitive and high-sensitive individuals. Transl Psychiatry, 8.

Nocentini, A., Menesini, E., & Pluess, M. (2018). The Personality Trait of Environmental Sensitivity Predicts Children’s Positive Response to School-Based Antibullying Intervention. Clinical Psychological Science, 6, 848-859.

Pluess, M., Aron, E.N., Kähkönen, J.E., Lionetti, F., Huang, Y., Tillmann, T., Greven, C.U., Aron, A. (2026). Evolution of the concept of sensory processing sensitivity and its measurement: The Highly Sensitive Person scale-revised, Personality and Individual Differences, 257

Schippers, L.M., Hoogman, M., Greven, C.U. (2025) Sensory processing sensitivity and the association with attention-deficit/ hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) traits, and ADHD-related strengths in the general population ,Current Research in Behavioral Sciences, 9.

Weyn S., Greven C.U., Schmidt S.J., Gillebert C.R., (2015). Sensory processing sensitivity and overstimulation in daily life: an experience sampling method study. Scientific Reports, 16.

#4638. Motorcycles are notoriously dangerous. Could electric motorcycles actually change that?

There’s no particularly comfortable way to talk about motorcycle safety. Motorcycles are dangerous. All the statistics point to the fact that per mile, motorcycles are significantly more dangerous. And as someone who promotes them as a better alternative to large cars and trucks for many trips, it’s an uncomfortable reality that must be grappled with.

But that simple statement also hides something important. Not all motorcycles, riders, or riding behaviors carry the same risk. And as a new generation of smaller electric motorcycles begins to emerge, I think there’s an interesting question worth asking: Could electric motorcycles inadvertently make motorcycling safer?

Not because electricity is somehow safer than gasoline. It isn’t. Rather, because electrification may fundamentally change the type of motorcycle that hits the road.

In 2024, 6,228 motorcyclists were killed in the US, accounting for 16% of all traffic fatalities, according to the NHTSA.

Obviously, motorcycles have a fundamental disadvantage here. You don’t have a steel cage around you. There aren’t crumple zones separating your body from an oncoming SUV. There’s no seatbelt holding you in place or curtain airbag waiting to catch your head.

But there’s another component to motorcycle fatalities that is harder to ignore: rider behavior.

Around 35% of motorcyclist deaths in 2024 occurred in single-vehicle crashes, according to the IIHS. In other words, more than one-third of those deaths didn’t involve a rider being hit by another vehicle. At that point, whether or not a crash occurred was essentially in the hands of the rider.

Alcohol is another major factor. Among riders killed in single-vehicle crashes, the NHTSA reports that 40% were alcohol-impaired.

Supersport motorcycles stand out for all the wrong reasons. Of the riders killed on supersports in 2024, 59% were under 30. Compare that to cruiser and standard motorcycles, where just 19% of killed riders were under 30, or touring motorcycles at only 7%.

That’s not proof that powerful motorcycles are causing those deaths, of course. There are all sorts of confounding factors, including the type of person attracted to different motorcycles and how those motorcycles tend to be ridden.

But it’s hard to ignore the broader picture.

To put it more plainly, a huge portion of motorcycle deaths are caused by riders simply going too fast, doing something wrong (like drinking or taking turns too aggressively), or because they couldn’t handle the power of an insanely high-performance crotch rocket. So while figures such as “motorcycles are 27x more deadly than cars” might be true in a broad sense, that doesn’t mean you have a 27x higher chance of death – especially not if you aren’t a 25-year-old hooligan on a second-hand liter bike.

One of the strange things about motorcycling is just how cheaply you can buy extraordinary performance.

Someone with relatively little riding experience can buy a used supersport capable of acceleration that would have required an exotic supercar not long ago. The motorcycle may weigh around 400 lb, produce well over 100 horsepower, and be capable of speeds approaching three times a typical US highway speed limit.

And unlike cars, there isn’t much protecting you when that performance gets away from you.

That’s why I find the current evolution of electric motorcycles so interesting.

For years, electric motorcycle companies largely chased gasoline motorcycles up the performance ladder. We got incredibly fast and powerful machines from companies like Energica and LiveWire.

Those bikes proved electric motorcycles could be fast.

But I’m increasingly interested in the opposite end of the spectrum.

Look at motorcycles such as LiveWire’s upcoming S4 Honcho.

This isn’t an electric superbike designed around insane acceleration or a 150 mph (240 km/h) top speed. It’s a smaller motorcycle intended to offer approachable performance at a more accessible price.

It adds to a growing market already populated by highly acclaimed modest-sized electric motorcycles like those from Ryvid, Land, and Maeving.

And we’re seeing more machines begin to occupy this previously neglected territory between an e-bike and a full-size motorcycle.

That could make a huge difference when it comes to overall safety, as crotch rockets get replaced by sensible electric motorbikes.

Battery technology actually creates an interesting incentive here. Making an electric motorcycle ridiculously powerful is easy. Giving it enough battery to sustain high speeds for long distances without becoming extremely heavy and expensive is much, much harder.

So the economics and physics of batteries naturally make smaller urban and suburban motorcycles fairly compelling right now.

Instead of asking how to build another 150 mph (240 km/h) electric motorcycle, manufacturers can build a lighter machine that goes 60 or 70 mph (95-120 km/h), has enough range for everyday riding, and costs considerably less.

Ironically, one of the limitations most commonly leveled against electric motorcycles could turn out to have a safety upside.

This is where I think things get even more interesting.

For decades, the stereotypical progression into motorcycling might have involved learning on a dirt bike or small displacement motorcycle, then moving fairly quickly into larger machines. Often though, new riders simply took a licensing course and then bought their first 600cc sport bike to learn to ride.

But now we’re raising an entirely new generation on electric two-wheelers.

Kids and teenagers are increasingly growing up riding e-bikes and small electric motos. Eventually, many of them are going to want something faster than a 20 or 28 mph e-bike.

A 50 mph (80 km/h) electric motorcycle is a pretty logical next step for the e-moto kids of today. Eventually, perhaps that rider graduates to something capable of 70 or 80 mph (120-130 km/h) and comfortable highway travel.

That’s a much more gradual performance curve than jumping from essentially no powered two-wheeler experience to a screaming 600cc supersport.

There’s another advantage too: electric motorcycles are mechanically easier to operate. There’s generally no clutch, no gearbox, and no concern about stalling. Twist the throttle and go.

That doesn’t necessarily make them safer – instant electric torque can certainly get an inexperienced rider into trouble – but it does remove several tasks from the mental workload of learning to ride.

The rider can spend more attention on braking, cornering, traffic, positioning, and the thousand other things that actually keep you alive on a motorcycle. The reduction in cognitive load can mean more focus on control, if it’s used that way.

To be clear, I’m not arguing that electric motorcycles are inherently safe.

They’re still motorcycles and they still lack cages. Well, most of them.

If an inattentive driver turns left in front of you, the chemistry powering your rear wheel isn’t going to make much difference.

And electric motorcycles can be outrageously powerful. In fact, the instantaneous torque of an electric motor can make poor throttle calibration especially unforgiving for inexperienced riders.

There also simply isn’t enough data yet to demonstrate that electric motorcycles have meaningfully lower fatality rates than comparable gasoline motorcycles.

My argument is that electrification may change what we consider a normal beginner motorcycle. And that could be much more important, helping to significantly reduce accidents and deaths.

I’m never going to pretend motorcycles can become as safe as cars. The physics simply don’t work that way.

But the broad statistic of “motorcycles are dangerous” encompasses an enormous spectrum of machines and riders.

A sober, trained commuter wearing proper protective gear and riding a modestly powered motorcycle to work is doing something fundamentally different from an inexperienced 21-year-old seeing how fast his supersport can take an empty freeway ramp at 2 a.m.

Yet both contribute to the same broad motorcycle fatality statistics.

What excites me about this emerging generation of electric motorcycles isn’t that swapping gasoline for batteries magically fixes motorcycle safety. It obviously doesn’t.

I bought a motorcycle around age 60 after considering the risk factors I could control:

I took a MSF basic riding course before buying the motorcycle. Best investment in the whole saga.

I always rode with full protection. That was doable but inconvenient and seriously uncomfortable in hot weather.

I never rode in rainy weather or at night. Again possible but limited my use of the motorcycle for commuting. Eventually my schedule changed to evening and stopped my motorcycle commuting altogether.

After a few close calls I started avoiding roads with more than one lane in each direction. That added quite a bit to my commute time.

I never rode when I was in a hurry. That meant more days I didn't use the motorcycle for commuting.

None of these precautions have anything to do with electric drive. After I sold my gas motorcycle I test rode an electric motorcycle and loved it. However I didn't buy it because it didn't reduce any of the risks and I wouldn't ride it more than the gas bike.

It’s that electrification could help create a new category of desirable, affordable motorcycles that don’t need 120 horsepower and a 160 mph top speed to be cool.

If younger riders grow up progressing from e-bikes to small e-motos and then to highway-capable electric motorcycles, perhaps we’ll wind up with a generation that sees a lightweight 60 or 70 mph motorcycle as a perfectly legitimate machine rather than merely a stepping stone to something ridiculously powerful.

Maybe electrification’s biggest contribution to motorcycle safety won’t be traction control, ABS, or sophisticated electronics.

Maybe it’ll simply make sensible motorcycles fun and cool again.

#4637. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: The Good and the Hard of Life on GLP-1s

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

“Years of diets that worked for a couple of months, then gave all the weight back and more. Now the food noise has gone quiet,” a GLP-1 user shared.

In June, our brilliant News team published a piece about actor Mayim Bialik and her challenging experience with GLP-1 side effects. It did well, like many of the celebrity + health condition + human-interest angle features we create tend to do with our audience (that’s you all reading this!). Not a massive viral hit by any measure, but a strong performer on the traffic front.

Jump forward nearly 4 months; our equally brilliant social media team posts the piece on Facebook, leading with one of Bialik’s quotes from the article: “GLP-1s have helped people in serious need. Of that I am certain. But nobody talks much about what happens when it goes wrong.”

The fuse was lit. Nearly 12k likes, 1k reposts, and 3.5k comments later, the team had their most engaged post of the year by some margin. The irony is not lost on me that Bialik’s quote, about how rarely people talk about side effects, sparked such a deep conversation about that very thing.

GLP-1s are a big topic for Healthline. They drive traffic, they drive revenue, and they offer a rich seam of human-centric storytelling for our teams. Even so, no one predicted the post would catch fire the way it did. Our social team’s read is that a few things stacked up: Mayim Bialik is a name our Facebook audience knows, the topic is one where nearly everyone has a stake, and a busy thread tends to get shown to more people, who then add more comments. That’s the hypothesis. What we’ve consistently seen is that posts that lead with a quote get more people talking than those that lead with a headline. You may have noticed this article takes the same approach.

We also know that the comment sections on social media aren’t always the most hospitable of environments, particularly in the health space. What stood out about the lion’s share of the comments we read was how constructive the discourse was. People were leading with deeply personal and often moving perspectives about the life changing impact (for good and bad) of GLP-1s. In turn, they were met with equally balanced and thoughtful responses.

Many of the comments expanded on Bialik’s experience, detailing long and difficult battles with a range of side effects. But plenty told the other side of the story: years of failed diets and struggles with chronic conditions leading to despondency, side effects that went on to ease with time, and life changing results that were ultimately worth the cost.

The line that opened this piece could have come from any of those commenters. It didn’t. It came from Kitty Hough, who is 75 and lives in London. Eagle-eyed readers will have spotted that she has the same surname as me – that’s because she’s my mom. She’s one of two people closer to the Healthline home who spoke to me for this piece and whose stories echo the Facebook post thread, with the good and the hard bits side by side.

Kitty was a hockey player and distance runner as a girl, the kind who could eat what she liked without it showing. Then came children, and a weight that crept up year after year, with decades of diets that “worked for a couple of months only to be back to my former weight and then some.” In late 2024, after a lot of research, she decided to try tirzepatide.

Since then, Kitty has lost 56 pounds. She says her joints hurt less, which she puts down to reduced inflammation. She is more mobile. The constant chatter about food has faded. She thinks harder before she eats now.

“I am a strong believer that obesity is a disease and in my case certainly not the result of overindulgence or laziness,” she says. “GLP-1s have greatly improved my health and self-esteem. After years of struggling with my weight, I have finally found a way to solve the problem.”

Kitty will also tell you what it cost. Nausea. Constipation. Sulfur-tasting burps and rough nights of indigestion. Initial hair loss that has since grown back, and loose skin. Muscle loss. And she misses some of the true joy of cooking and eating food.

But despite bumps in her journey, Kitty remains convinced that the benefits of GLP-1s for her life and health outweigh any drawbacks she’s experienced. “I am conscious that I will probably be on this drug for a long time if not for life. It is truly a miracle drug.”

I also spoke to Ann Marie Maguire, AGNP-C, RN, TCTCN, a nurse practitioner specializing in transplantation and cellular therapy, the sister of Healthline’s Chief Business Officer Christine Macguire, and someone who has lost over 50lbs since starting GLP-1s in 2022.

“I struggled with my weight since my teens and always believed I should be able to manage it on my own. But in my 30s, my knees were hurting just getting out of bed or walking to dinner. I realized how much my weight was affecting my quality of life. Starting a GLP-1 in 2022, alongside healthier eating and exercise, made a tremendous difference. My only regret is not starting sooner,” said Ann Marie.

As a healthcare professional, Ann Marie also identified cost as a major factor that can’t be ignored regarding GLP-1s and their impact.

“There’s understandable debate about the long-term use and cost of these medications,” she says. “But we also need to consider the health and financial burden of obesity, including cardiovascular complications, hospitalizations, surgeries and ongoing medications. The cost conversation should account for the potential benefits of preventing or reducing those complications.”

Ann Marie points to a frustration many patients will recognize: reaching a healthier weight can become the reason coverage gets cut off. “We don’t automatically stop blood pressure medication because a patient’s readings improve,” she says. The treatment may be what’s keeping the condition controlled. Obesity, she argues, deserves the same approach. “Reaching a goal weight can mean treatment is working, and decisions about continuing it should reflect the patient’s ongoing needs, benefits and side effects.”

It’s important to note that this article looks at the experiences of only a handful of people out of the millions who now take GLP-1s. Like all drugs, these medications are not right for everyone. Side effects are common; some of them can be serious, and both the long-term impact and what happens when people stop are still being worked out. Ultimately, your care team, with knowledge of your medical history, is a far better guide than a comment thread.

Yet the evidence now reaches well beyond the scales: large trials have linked semaglutide to fewer heart attacks and strokes in people with heart disease and slower kidney decline in people with diabetes and kidney disease, and tirzepatide became the first FDA-approved drug for moderate to severe sleep apnea in adults with obesity.

Stories like Kitty’s, Ann Marie’s, Mayim Bialik’s, and those of the 3.5k commenters on the Facebook post aren’t proof of what will happen to you one way or another. But for a lot of people, my mom included, these drugs have changed what an ordinary day looks like, and in many cases changed what their future can look like.

One of the most significant drug developments of the century so far? Hard to argue with.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

The most affordable Volkswagen ID. Polo Trend starts at just €24,995, or about $27,500, but you’ll have to wait close to two years to get one.

The new ID. Polo is “an affordable friend for everyday life,” as Volkswagen’s chief designer Andreas Mindt calls it.

After opening orders for the ID. Polo with the 52 kWh battery at the end of April, starting at 33,795 euros ($37,000), Volkswagen made good on its promise, launching the lower-priced, smaller-battery model in July.

The VW ID. Polo Trend with the 37 kWh battery went on sale in Europe in July, starting at just 24,995 euros, or about $27,500, with a WLTP range of 207 miles (334 km).

By mid-September, reports claimed Volkswagen’s entry-level EV was already essentially sold out across actross all trims, with more than 30,000 orders and a 10-month waitlist.

According to the latest update from German automotive news outlet Edison Media, that number has doubled in about two months, and buyers now face delivery times of up to 21 months for the base ID. Polo Trend. Deliveries for the sporty GTI version are expected to be around seven months.

“We clearly planned too conservatively,” a VW manager told Edison during an interview. While VW expected about 90 to 95% to choose to lease, the leasing rate is only about 50%.

The larger 52 kWh battery version has also seen higher-than-expected demand, while 90% surprisingly opted to buy the optional €810 ($890) detachable towbar.

As a result, the company is prioritizing higher-margin models, which is likely leading to longer delivery times for the base ID. Polo.

The entry-level variants “just clog up to the line,” Volkswagen’s manager said during the recent interview.

Demand for the ID. Cross, the electric equivalent to Volkswagen’s T-Cross, is also already exceeding expectations.

The issue here is that the thing in sold out at 30,000 Units. it out to have production capacity beyond 100K!

Volkswagen opened orders for the entry-level ID. Cross Trend last month, starting at €27,995 ($31,000) in Germany, including VAT. The 52 kWh battery version will go on sale in the UK this week, starting at £30,260 ($40,000). The ID. Cross Life with the 37 kWh battery will go on sale in January 2027, starting at £26,985 ($35,500).

Volkswagen’s new entry-level electric cars are off to a promising start. The electric urban car family, which includes the ID. Polo, ID. Cross, and the CUPRA Raval and Skoda Epiq, has received nearly 150,000 orders combined since production began in June.

However, the German automaker is still facing an uphill battle. The VW Group posted an operating loss of 5.9 billion euros ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter, its worst quarterly loss since the Dieselgate scandal.

In September, Volkswagen’s supervisory board approved its Future Plan 2030, which calls for reducing its global workforce by up to 100,000, closing plants, and narrowing its vehicle lineup to cut costs.

#4635. How to Cure the Grand Theft Auto-VI Craze: Get Kids Knitting

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

Grand Theft Auto VI has been dominating the lives of gamers, young and old, since its arrival on November 19th. It can seem impossible for parents to resist the inertia that settles on kids as they spend dozens (hundreds) of hours in front of screens engaged in violent role-play. While there is no easy solution, with the holidays fast approaching and gift-giving on many parents' minds, maybe there is a quaint solution to this very technological problem. Knitting.

A few months ago I was presenting to an audience in northern Norway where I observed something odd. At least 10% of my audience were knitting. These weren’t church ladies with white hair and compression socks (what an awful stereotype but sadly one that is portrayed far too often in our popular culture). My audience of knitters comprised, instead, younger women and men who were listening attentively to what I was saying while occupying their hands with needles and skeins of yarn. Where it has become routine to put stress balls and fidget toys on conference room tables, here was a much nicer way to evoke calm. Even better, the repetition wasn’t a wasted act of self-flagellation. My audience was engaged in a creative activity that turned a ball of wool into gifts for children or casual sofa throws for lovers and friends.

Why don’t we teach children to knit anymore? For that matter, why has it become so rare to see a child whittling with a pocket knife, sewing, building a tree fort, painting their room, drawing a tree, or creating something that is three-dimensional, tactile? So few children experience a distraction that has purpose and a tangible outcome. Video games are the opposite. Time consuming with no discernible gain.

If this sounds like nonsensical nostalgia, it’s not. There is good reason to believe that one part of the solution to our children’s mental health crisis is to be found in encouraging them to do arts and crafts and other do-it-yourself (DIY) activities like woodwork and gardening. In a study of 18-24-year-olds recruited (ironically) online, those who were more engaged in extracurricular activities, including crafts, reported significantly lower risk for suicide and a greater sense of belongingness, two outcomes that are co-dependent.

That same pattern was found during the COVID-19 pandemic when some 3,725 adults were surveyed in the USA, with a clear pattern to the findings. Those who gardened, those who did woodwork, and those who immersed themselves regularly in arts and crafts all reported lower rates of mental health problems.

While we adults obviously see these benefits, our children may, if given the opportunity, tell us that having some fun activities to do that don’t involve screens is actually welcomed. That was the message from a 2022 report that included over 7,000 kids in Finland where, to be honest, being outdoors and working with one’s hands is more a part of the culture than in North America. Still, it seems that kids who are encouraged to engage in non-screen activities can realize a nice mental health bump.

I can certainly relate to these findings. I’ve always been someone who liked to work with my hands. I am an avid woodworker, but also knit, sew and draw. I can remember well the feeling as a child of accomplishing something concrete and sharing it with others. The reflected glory of being seen as a maker was wonderful.

It’s up to us adults to not just take screens away from kids but to also provide the resources to keep them occupied. That might be an easel and paint, a saw and workbench, a garden or maybe a pet. And yes, it could even be a set of knitting needles and some brightly colored yarn.

Bauer, B. W., Capron, D. W., Ward-Ciesielski, E., Gustafsson, H. C., & Doyle, C. (2017). Extracurricular Activities are Associated with Lower Suicidality through Decreased Thwarted Belongingness in Young Adults. Archives of Suicide Research, 22(4), 665–678. https://doi.org/10.1080/13811118.2018.1427162

Bone, J. K., Fancourt, D., Sonke, J. K., Fluharty, M. E., Cohen, R., Lee, J. B., Kolenic, A. J., Radunovich, H., & Bu, F. (2023). Creative leisure activities, mental health and well-being during 5 months of the COVID-19 pandemic: a fixed effects analysis of data from 3725 US adults. Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health (1979), 77(5), 293–297. https://doi.org/10.1136/jech-2022-219653

MENA (2022). Children and young people want investments in hobbies, school and health: Report. https://ezproxy.library.dal.ca/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/wire-…

#4633. Getting More Physical Activity May Help With Your Perimenopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new study found that exercising more frequently may help alleviate perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes, anxiety, and urinary issues.

The study results were recently presented at The Menopause Society’s 2026 Annual Conference.

Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause.

Due to hormonal changes that mark the end of a person’s reproductive years, symptoms like hot flashes, mood swings, brain fog, insomnia, and urinary incontinence are common.

Past studies show that lifestyle modifications, such as eating a healthy diet, managing stress, and getting enough physical activity, can help reduce some perimenopause symptoms.

“Physical activity is low cost, accessible, and already known to benefit sleep, mood, and heart and bone health — all areas that matter a great deal during perimenopause,” said study lead and co-author Liudmila Zhaunova, PhD, director of science at Flo Health — the developer of a women’s health tracking app, which was used to collect health data for this study. “But when we looked at the research, there was surprisingly little evidence specific to perimenopause.”

“Hormone therapy isn’t suitable or desired for everyone, so women deserve a broader set of evidence-based options,” Zhaunova told Healthline. “The more we understand about accessible, lifestyle-based approaches, the better equipped women and their healthcare providers are to build a plan that works for them.”

Study researchers recruited more than 1,800 women from around the globe who were using the Flo app.

Study participants were asked to complete online surveys about their physical activity, from not being physically active to exercising more than 5 days a week.

Participants were also asked to report on their perimenopause symptoms in three categories — somatic (body-based issues like hot flashes), psychological (mental health issues like mood changes), and urogenital (issues regarding the urinary or vaginal areas). Researchers rated the severity of these symptoms using the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS).

The researchers found that higher rates of physical activity were associated with fewer perimenopausal symptoms across all three categories.

“Perimenopause symptoms are wide-ranging, and women often experience several at once,” Zhaunova said. “Seeing a lower symptom burden across all three domains suggests that being more active may be relevant to women’s overall experience, not just one symptom.”

Additionally, the scientists discovered that the greatest exercise benefit was observed in the reduction of perimenopausal psychological symptoms.

“Psychological symptoms, such as low mood, irritability, anxiety, and exhaustion, are among the most disruptive parts of perimenopause, and they’re often overlooked or not recognized as related to this life stage,” Zhaunova explained.

“Our findings suggest that physical activity may matter most for mood and anxiety-related symptoms,” she continued.

“This could help women and clinicians have more informed conversations about how to support mental well-being during perimenopause. That said, women with more symptoms may find it harder to exercise, so we need further research to understand the direction of the relationship.”

Sherry Ross, MD, a board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, said that regular exercise could potentially help relieve perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes and mood changes. Ross wasn’t involved in this study, but noted other benefits of exercising during this life stage:

“Exercise releases endorphins, improves blood vessel health, lowers inflammation, helps reset circadian rhythm, and improves the body’s internal cooling system,” Ross told Healthline. “Collectively, these changes ease anxiety, irritability, mood changes, sleep, and fatigue.”

“There were mixed reviews on how exercise benefits hot flashes, but exercise does help with weight control, which may benefit hot flashes,” she said. “Strengthening the pelvic floor and core may help with the urinary symptoms women many experience in perimenopause.”

Prudence Hall, MD, an OB-GYN in private practice in Santa Monica, CA, and author of “Radiant Again & Forever,” said that building a sustainable exercise routine requires consistency, joy, and community. Hall wasn’t involved in the study, but shared some exercise tips for perimenopausal women.

“Too often in midlife, previously stable women suddenly plummet into deep depression and anxiety, only to be prescribed multiple medications with debilitating side effects that never address the underlying biology,” Hall said.

“While hormone optimization remains essential to correct these endocrine deficiencies, exercise serves as a powerful, non-pharmaceutical therapy that directly targets the true root causes by revitalizing our cellular health and restoring overall vitality.”

#4632. Tesla Cybercab has crashed 8 times, and the data shows a speed problem

Tesla’s Cybercab now has 8 crashes on file with NHTSA, barely two months after the purpose-built robotaxi started giving public rides in Austin.

Four happened in driverless “Robotaxi” service, and none topped 5 mph. The other four happened with a test driver on board and Tesla’s driver-assist engaged, including one where a Cybercab hit a car at 53 mph on a highway in Philadelphia.

The data points at what we think is the biggest limitation of Tesla’s self-driving program right now: speed.

Tesla files Cybercab crashes under NHTSA’s Standing General Order in two separate datasets.

The first is the ADS (Automated Driving System) file, which covers Level 4 driverless operation. That’s the Robotaxi service, where nobody is in the driver’s seat. NHTSA’s latest ADS release, published this month, contains 43 unique Tesla reports, up from 22 in July. Four are Cybercabs:

Those are minor. Two weren’t Tesla’s fault at all, and none involved an injury.

The second bucket is the Level 2 ADAS file, which covers driver-assist systems like Autopilot and “Full Self-Driving” (Supervised). Tesla has been testing Cybercabs fitted with steering wheels and a human behind them, often in places where it has no Robotaxi permit. Those crashes land in the ADAS file, with the driver type coded “In-Vehicle (Commercial / Test)” and the system “Verified Engaged.”

There are four of them, all in September 2026:

Tesla redacted the narrative of all four as confidential business information, so there’s no way to tell from the public data who was at fault or what the system was doing. Pennsylvania State Police, Austin Police, Lehi Police, and Florida Highway Patrol are listed as the investigating agencies.

The Philadelphia crash is not the Broad Street crash where a Cybercab lost its door panel that we reported in October. That one happened on a city street in October. This one happened on a highway in September, at around 10 p.m. local time.

Tesla has no permit to run automated vehicles in Pennsylvania, and it doesn’t run Robotaxi in Utah either. In Utah, a Cybercab was photographed in Park City in September with a driver visible behind the wheel.

Two of the eight Cybercab crashes involved injuries. Both are in the Level 2 file.

Across all 43 Tesla Robotaxi reports in the ADS file, the highest pre-crash speed is 29 mph. That was a driverless Model Y with two riders hitting a pothole in Dallas in September, after which one rider said they sought medical care. The median speed across all 43 reports is 1 mph.

Not one of those 43 crashes happened on a highway. Tesla coded 21 on streets, 15 in parking lots, and 7 at intersections.

Those numbers say more about where Tesla lets the system drive than about the software itself. As we reported last month, Robotaxi sticks to low-speed routes inside small geofenced zones and largely stays off highways.

The Robotaxi Safety Report Tesla published on October 21 claims zero people injured by Robotaxi over 3,112,541 driverless miles between January 22 and October 18. It doesn’t mention the Cybercab’s test fleet, and it excludes every mile driven with a safety monitor on board.

Take the speed cap off and the picture changes.

In the Level 2 data, Teslas with Autopilot or FSD engaged regularly crash at highway speeds. Our master dataset of Tesla’s ADAS reports holds 69 fatal crashes. Among the 52 where Tesla recorded a speed, the median was 53 mph, the same speed the Cybercab was going in Philadelphia, and 29 happened at 50 mph or more.

Today alone, we matched three fatal crashes to Tesla’s latest filings:

Engagement within 30 seconds of a crash, which is what triggers these reports, doesn’t prove the system caused it. But the pattern is consistent. At low speeds in a tight geofence, Tesla’s crashes are scrapes with chains, curbs, and potholes. At highway speeds, they can kill.

The Cybercab test fleet is where those two worlds overlap. It’s the same vehicle Tesla runs driverless in Austin, and the one Cybercab crash on record at real speed happened at 53 mph on a Philadelphia highway.

The Cybercab’s four driverless crashes are minor, and some weren’t Tesla’s fault. No one is denying that. But minor crashes still count, and so do the four Level 2 crashes that Tesla’s “zero injuries” framing leaves out. Both datasets describe the same vehicle running Tesla’s self-driving software.

It's looked to me for a while now that many of the improvements that people feel when they use FSD is not just the system getting better, but Elon pulling off the guardrails so the system attempts to do more stuff.

What the data shows is that Tesla has a speed problem. Its Robotaxi service looks clean largely because Tesla keeps it slow, off highways, and inside small zones. That’s also what makes it far less useful than a real ride-hailing service. You can’t take a Cybercab to the airport if the airport is on the other side of a freeway.

To be clear, we think Tesla is right to do it this way. Given what the Level 2 data shows at 50+ mph, letting driverless Cybercabs onto highways today would be reckless.

But it means the hard part is still ahead. Highways, larger geofences, and higher speeds are where crashes become fatal, and that’s where Tesla needs its system to be nearly perfect before it can scale. The Cybercab’s test crashes suggest it isn’t there yet. The question is how long Tesla can keep growing a robotaxi network that can’t go fast.

#4631. Who Stays, and Who Goes, in New Research on Relationships

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Your neighbors have been married for years, almost to the point where you can’t imagine them as anything but together. Much to your surprise, they come by to let you know that they're done. Here you thought you were a pretty good judge of character, if not love, but clearly you’ve missed some clues.

As it turns out, relationship researchers can be in the same thorny situation. The holy grail in investigations of divorce is to find the magic formula that predicts who sticks it out and who moves on from a long-term partner. A newly published study provides some hope that the grail may yet be achieved.

University of California Los Angeles’ Molly Smith and colleagues (2026) took advantage of a 12-year longitudinal data set involving 368 newlywed couples who were studied 10 times on a yearly or near-yearly basis. The purpose of the study was to contrast three perspectives on the development of married couples, including the possible outcome of divorce. The authors contrasted these three theoretical perspectives on relationship development to see which would prove strongest:

Over the course of the 12-year period, couples completed individual interviews as well as participated in behavioral observations during discussion of a contentious topic, chosen by the couples. The topics they discussed included finances, household chores, family obligations, and communication during conflict management.

Coders rated the videos of each component of the behavioral observations along the dimensions of positive and negative adaptive communication. Positivity included such observations as positive mood, warmth/support, physical affection, humor, enjoyment, endearment, and responsiveness. The negativity ratings included disruptive responses, hostility, contempt, denial, angry coercion, dominance, verbal attack, interrogation, and externalized negative behavior. A third set of ratings assessed effective communication (e.g., coming up with good solutions).

In the statistical model testing these contributions to divorce, the main finding to emerge was that the vulnerabilities of wives was the strongest contributor. This included adverse childhood experiences, parental divorce, history of abuse, negative emotions, and problematic substance use. Indeed, wives’ vulnerability was the only significant predictor of time to divorce.

In interpreting this finding, one possibility the authors offer is that women are more tuned in to relationship problems so that, when something bad occurs, they will be the first to leave. Social role theory proposes, in contrast, that women are expected more than men are to take on the larger share of labor in the household as well as to maintain intimacy. Vulnerability adds to the likelihood of seeking divorce because, in the words of the authors, “vulnerable women may more readily reach a threshold of dissatisfaction that prompts a decision to exit.”

These explanations can only go so far, however. Even the best predictive model only performed at 34 percent accuracy. Sometimes couples just decide to split, which the authors suggest may not be the worst outcome in a bad relationship.

Even though the outcome of divorce was not predicted with a high degree of certainty, there were mitigating effects of good communication on relationship outcome for vulnerable wives. If a couple communicated well, this could “neutralize the risk conferred by wives’ vulnerabilities.”

Looking at your own relationship, the findings suggest you might want to look to external threats to your relationship rather than communication strategies alone. Returning to the example of your neighbors, couples who seem to get along well may still face an uphill battle in cases when the vulnerability of the wife due to external factors becomes overly burdensome.

The findings can also help you gain perspective on the difficulty of peeking inside a marriage or other long-term committed relationship to know what’s going on. Even with as meticulous a method as Smith et al. used, it wasn’t possible to overcome low odds in predicting who divorced. The authors also point out that what plays out in the lives of newlyweds may be very different than what occurs over the course of time. Stressors such as financial difficulties can develop over time to erode what may have looked like a great relationship at the outset.

To sum up, foretelling long-term couple outcomes is a science fraught with difficulties. The UCLA study suggests that looking outside as well as inside the relationship may ultimately improve that science.

For more on this topic, check out this previous post on what can ruin a good relationship.

Smith, M. G., Block, J. M., Bradbury, T. N., & Karney, B. R. (2026). Individual, interpersonal, and socioeconomic predictors of divorce: A 12-year prospective study. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/pspi0000537
